caption:
Your bones are stronger than concrete. 🦴

Squeeze test:
House concrete cracks at about 20-30 MPa
Bone tissue holds about 200 MPa
That's around 6x more

But hit a bone from the side and it breaks much easier: bone is strongest when squeezed along its length.
And unlike concrete, bone is alive. It repairs itself.

Send this to the friend who thinks they're made of glass.

Source: Reilly & Burstein, Journal of Biomechanics 1975 (human cortical bone); standard strength of residential concrete.

#nexthuman #bones #anatomy #bodyfacts #science

caption:
You fall into ice water. The first minute decides. 🧊

The 1-10-1 rule:
1 minute: cold shock. You gasp and hyperventilate. Control your breathing.
10 minutes: of useful movement before your arms stop working
1 hour: before hypothermia knocks you out

Most cold-water deaths happen before hypothermia. So don't panic-swim: float, slow your breathing, then get out.

Send this to the friend who swims in winter.

Source: Prof. Gordon Giesbrecht, University of Manitoba (1-10-1 principle).

caption:
You wake up. Your body doesn't. 😶
It's called sleep paralysis.

In dream sleep (REM), your brain switches off your muscles so you don't act out your dreams.
Sometimes you wake up before the switch turns back on.
Many people see a figure in the room or feel weight on their chest.
About 28% of students have had it at least once (about 8% of people overall).

It's harmless and usually over in a few minutes.

Send this to the friend who saw someone at night.

Source: Sharpless & Barber, Sleep Medicine Reviews 2011 (35 studies, 36,533 people).

caption:
An ice bath after the gym can slow your gains. 🧊💪

The study: 21 active men lifted twice a week for 12 weeks.
After every session, one group sat 10 minutes in cold water (about 10°C), the other did an active cool-down.
After 12 weeks, the cold group gained less muscle and less strength.
Fast muscle fibres grew 17% only in the group without ice.

Cold may still help sore muscles. The catch is the timing.

Send this to the friend who ice baths after leg day.

Source: Roberts et al., The Journal of Physiology 2015 (University of Queensland).

caption:
Your brain fills your skull. His was mostly fluid. 🧠

A 44-year-old man in France saw doctors for a weak leg.
His scan showed huge fluid-filled spaces and a very thin layer of brain.
He had hydrocephalus since he was a baby, treated with a shunt at 6 months.
He worked as a civil servant, was married and had two kids. His IQ was 75.

His brain wasn't missing: it was squeezed, and it kept working.

Send this to the friend who says they have no brain.

Source: Feuillet, Dufour & Pelletier, The Lancet 2007, "Brain of a white-collar worker".

caption:
In a vacuum, the spit on your tongue boils. One man felt it. 🫧

December 1966, NASA, Houston: Jim LeBlanc was testing a spacesuit in a vacuum chamber.
His air hose came loose. The pressure dropped to what you'd face at about 120,000 feet.
He felt the saliva on his tongue bubbling, then he blacked out.
Engineers repressurised the chamber in 87 seconds.

He woke up with no long-term effects.

Send this to the friend who wants to go to space.

Source: Guinness World Records, Highest equivalent altitude exposure survived (NASA, 1966).

caption:
6 months in space. Now you can't walk straight. 🧑‍🚀

Up there, your balance system stops using gravity.
Your weight-bearing bones lose about 1-1.5% a month, and your muscles shrink.
Back on Earth, your brain has to relearn gravity: balance and walking can take weeks to recover.
In one study, some astronauts' shinbones still hadn't fully recovered a year later.

Send this to the friend who wants to live on Mars.

Source: npj Microgravity meta-analysis 2020; University of Calgary study of 17 astronauts (Scientific Reports 2022); Frontiers in Neurology review 2025.

caption:
Your nails don't keep growing after you die. 🖐️

At 1-2 hours: muscles start to stiffen (rigor mortis)
By 6-12 hours: fully stiff
In 1-2 days: it fades
Then: the skin dries and shrinks back, so nails and hair look longer

No energy, no new cells, no growth. The tip stays exactly where it was.

Send this to the friend who still believes it.

Source: Medscape, Postmortem Changes; Live Science on the 2007 BMJ medical myths study.

#nexthuman #myth #bodyfacts #anatomy #science

caption:
Your coffee doesn't give you energy. ☕

While you're awake, a chemical called adenosine builds up in your brain. It's the "tired" signal.
Caffeine blocks the receptors that read it. The tiredness is still there, you just can't feel it.
About half the caffeine is still in your body around 5 hours later (it varies a lot from person to person).
When it wears off, the tiredness was there all along.

Send this to the friend on their third coffee.

Source: StatPearls (NCBI), Caffeine; Emma Beckett, University of Newcastle.

#nexthuman #caffeine #coffee #sleep #science

First hours: it uses the sugar stored in your liver
Around 12-24 hours: that store runs low and fat takes over

Timings vary a lot with what you ate before, how active you are and your metabolism.

Above 8,000 m, your body is slowly dying. 🏔️

On top of Everest (8,849 m), each breath brings about a third of the oxygen you'd get at sea level.
Up there your body can't adapt: it only gets worse the longer you stay.
That's why most climbers breathe bottled oxygen.
But on 8 May 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler reached the top without it.

Send this to the friend who wants to climb Everest.

Source: Guinness World Records, first ascent of Everest without supplementary oxygen; high-altitude physiology (Himalayan Database).

#nexthuman #everest #altitude #mountains #science

caption:
Your urge to breathe isn't about oxygen. 🫁

When you hold your breath, CO2 builds up in your blood.
That burning feeling is your body's CO2 alarm.
Hyperventilate first and you lower your CO2, so the alarm comes later.
But oxygen can run out first, and you can pass out without warning.

Never practise breath holds in water alone.

Send this to the friend who holds their breath in the pool.

Source: physiology of the control of breathing; shallow water blackout safety warnings.

#nexthuman #breathing #freediving #watersafety #science

caption:
On the Moon without a suit, you wouldn't explode. 🌕

Your skin is strong enough to hold you together.
But you'd swell, and the air would rush out of your lungs.
In about 10-15 seconds, you'd black out from lack of oxygen.
A few minutes later, your brain would shut down.

Send this to the friend who wants a ticket to the Moon.

Source: ESA engineer Stefaan De Mey; NASA Human Research Program (Kris Lehnhardt), via Space.com and Live Science.

#nexthuman #moon #space #nasa #science
first_comment: In 1966 one NASA engineer went through this in a test chamber and survived. Tomorrow: more about what your body can survive 🧬
